answer: Selection into treatment occurs when the units that receive a treatment differ systematically from those that do not, so that treatment assignment is related to outcomes for reasons other than the treatment itself. Before comparing outcomes, economists ask what determines which units get treated. In this CAPHE lab, wealthier California counties with more health infrastructure are far more likely to adopt a maternal health program and already have lower mortality, so a simple treated-versus-untreated comparison confounds the program's effect with selection. The fix is not more sophisticated adjustment but finding sources of treatment variation unrelated to potential outcomes.

faqs.a: It is when units receiving treatment differ systematically from those that do not. It creates bias when the characteristics driving treatment adoption are also related to the outcome, so comparisons mix the treatment effect with selection.

faqs.q: Why does selection make program effects hard to scale?
faqs.a: If wealthy, well-resourced counties adopt a program and already have better outcomes, some benefit may be attributed to the program that would have happened anyway. Scaling to counties without those advantages may not replicate the observed results.

faqs.q: Can statistical controls eliminate selection bias?
faqs.a: Controls help but cannot eliminate bias from unmeasured factors that predict both adoption and outcomes. Selection on unobservables remains a fundamental threat that adjustment alone does not solve.

faqs.q: What does selection bias mean for the counterfactual?
faqs.a: We never observe what would have happened to treated units without treatment. Selection makes that counterfactual especially hard to estimate because treated and untreated units were not comparable to begin with.
